edits.before:
The factory fence separated the workforce from the city without separating either from the gas. Nearby residents and responders could be exposed through different routes, with different information and access to help. The emergency crossed boundaries that the administration of safety often treats separately.

Casualty estimates must retain their definitions. Immediate deaths, later deaths attributed to exposure and recorded injuries describe different outcomes and populations; adding them together does not produce a meaningful lifetime total.
edits.after:
The event makes a practical question unavoidable: who belongs inside a factory's safety plan when its hazards can reach people who do not work there? A property boundary cannot answer that question.

Casualty estimates must retain their definitions. Immediate deaths, later deaths attributed to exposure and recorded injuries are not interchangeable counts. Figures from separate reports should not be combined without reconciling their time periods, definitions and overlapping populations. Exposure and injury totals are not death totals.

edits.before: The ILO report was issued for World Day for Safety and Health at Work in April 2004. Its section on major accidents describes a runaway reaction involving stored methyl isocyanate at Bhopal and recognizes health consequences lasting well beyond the release. Its perspective is explicitly that of an organization concerned with preventing harm from work and industrial chemicals.
edits.after: The ILO report was issued for World Day for Safety and Health at Work in April 2004. Its section on major accidents places Bhopal within an argument for preventing harm from industrial chemicals. This is a retrospective safety report, not a clinical follow-up of each person exposed.

edits.before:
An industrial history can lose that distinction through a deceptively simple timeline: accident, response, settlement, end. The final entry is usually the end of a selected administrative process. Different questions need different timelines. The production history concerns one set of decisions. Emergency communication concerns another. Medical follow-up and the ability to obtain help concern people whose needs may outlast both.

Production, emergency communication and medical follow-up operate on different timelines. A settlement or a closed administrative case cannot establish that treatment needs or exposure questions have ended.
edits.after:
An industrial history can lose that distinction through a deceptively simple timeline: accident, response, settlement, end. Such a sequence can suggest closure even when its entries concern different questions. The production history concerns one set of decisions. Emergency communication concerns another. Medical follow-up and the ability to obtain help concern people whose needs may outlast both.

The distinction is methodological: a legal or administrative milestone answers the question assigned to that process. It does not, by itself, answer a medical or exposure question. Establishing what a particular settlement resolved would require its own legal record.

edits.before: The release stopped; its consequences continued. Medical care, exposure assessment and legal obligations ran on different timetables. Closing the plant's operating history could not close the history of those who had been exposed.
edits.after: The 2004 account records consequences extending beyond the release. It does not establish present-day health outcomes, contamination levels or unresolved legal obligations. Keeping those limits visible makes the historical point more precise: ending a release is not the same as accounting for everyone it reached.

edits.before:
The U.S. Public Health Service study at Tuskegee enrolled 600 Black men in 1932 without informed consent, according to CDC's history. Participants were not offered penicillin when it became an established treatment. The study continued until 1972.

Of the 600 men, 399 had late-latent syphilis and 201 did not. The figures do not establish that researchers infected participants. CDC's documented account concerns a different abuse: men were studied without informed consent and were not offered an established treatment.

### What the study needed
edits.after:
The U.S. Public Health Service study at Tuskegee ran from 1932 to 1972. CDC's history describes 600 Black men enrolled without informed consent. The men with syphilis were not offered penicillin through the study after it became an established treatment.

CDC identifies 399 men with pre-existing late-latent syphilis and 201 controls without the disease. It explicitly states that researchers did not deliberately infect the men. The distinction matters: the study's abuse involved deception, lack of informed consent and failure to offer treatment for a disease already present.

## What the study needed

edits.before:
### What the groups actually counted

CDC distinguishes 399 men who already had late-latent syphilis when recruited from a control group of 201 men without the disease. The total of 600 therefore does not mean 600 men with syphilis. This distinction changes what the study's population describes, while leaving the central ethical finding intact.
edits.after:
## What untreated meant

The [1973 advisory panel report](https://digirepo.nlm.nih.gov/ext/mm/2934097RX4/PDF/2934097RX4.pdf), on printed pages 7 and 10, adds a limit to the word untreated: some men received therapy from physicians outside the study, not necessarily in doses sufficient to treat syphilis. This does not establish that the study offered appropriate care. On page 12, the panel concluded that penicillin should have been made available no later than 1953.

edits.before: Penicillin changed the medical options. The study continued to pursue observations of untreated disease. Withholding treatment was therefore part of the research decision, not an absence of action outside the study.
edits.after: Penicillin changed the medical options. The study's failure to offer it was part of the research decision, not an absence of action outside the study. Therapy obtained elsewhere does not erase that responsibility.

edits.before:
### A release has an information trail

HSE describes a reactor's bursting disc rupturing around 12:37 on 10 July. A visible cloud left the plant, carrying TCDD among its constituents. The case history states that the release lasted about twenty minutes and that confusion followed because communication between the company and authorities was inadequate.
edits.after:
## A release has an information trail

The twenty-minute estimate describes the release, not the duration of anyone's exposure. A description of the cloud does not establish an individual's dose or later diagnosis. Those questions need separate exposure and health evidence.

edits.before:
The distinction also changes how a technical safeguard is evaluated. Relieving pressure can protect a vessel while directing its contents somewhere else. The safety question must follow that route to its destination. A device cannot be judged solely by whether the equipment immediately around it survives.

HSE's account establishes an offsite release accompanied by inadequate communication. Residents' instructions, their timing and their reception require separate response records and testimony.

### A place has more than one recovery date
edits.after:
The distinction also changes how a technical safeguard is evaluated. HSE records that no equipment collected or destroyed the vented toxic material and that a recovery receiver recommended by the bursting-disc manufacturer was not fitted. A pressure-relief device and a system for containing its discharge serve different purposes. Protecting a vessel is not, by itself, protection for people downwind.

HSE's page is a retrospective accident summary that cites a 1996 loss-prevention text. It supports this bounded process and communication account. Residents' instructions, their timing and their reception require separate response records and testimony; the summary cannot substitute for them.
